regions.name: the Humber
facts: Hornsea, off the Yorkshire coast, is one of the largest offshore wind farms in the world.
Wind turbine blades for the North Sea are made in Hull.
The Humber’s ports and refineries are developing hydrogen and carbon capture projects.

topics.Wind energy: Uses Hornsea offshore wind farm as the worked example, with blade-making in Hull.
topics.Electricity: Follows electricity from Hornsea’s turbines to homes across Yorkshire.
topics.Energy transfers: Traces energy from North Sea wind to the National Grid via the Humber.
topics.Chemical reactions: Links hydrogen production to low-carbon projects on the Humber.

regions.default: Swaps in examples from the Humber’s ports, energy and engineering industries.
regions.demoLine: Hornsea, off the Yorkshire coast, is one of the world’s largest offshore wind farms. Its blades are made just up the river in Hull.

regions.name: Aberdeen
facts: Aberdeen is known as the UK’s energy capital after decades of North Sea oil and gas.
Its energy industry is moving towards offshore wind, hydrogen and carbon capture.
Much of the city is built from local granite, giving it the name the Granite City.

topics.Wind energy: Uses offshore wind farms off the Aberdeenshire coast as the worked example.
topics.Electricity: Follows electricity from North Sea wind farms to homes in the North East.
topics.Energy transfers: Compares North Sea oil and gas with the region’s new wind and hydrogen energy.
topics.Chemical reactions: Connects fuels and hydrogen to the North Sea energy industry.
topics.Rocks and fossils: Uses Aberdeen’s granite buildings to explore igneous rock.

regions.default: Swaps in examples from Aberdeen’s energy industry and the North Sea.
regions.demoLine: Aberdeen has powered the UK for decades from the North Sea. Today, wind farms off the Aberdeenshire coast are part of that story.

regions.name: Glasgow
facts: Glasgow builds more small satellites than any other city in Europe.
The River Clyde has a long history of shipbuilding and engineering.
Fossil Grove in Victoria Park preserves tree stumps over 300 million years old.

topics.Space: Uses satellites built in Glasgow as the real-world example.
topics.Rocks and fossils: Adds an activity on Fossil Grove in Victoria Park.
topics.Materials: Links materials to ship and satellite engineering on the Clyde.
topics.Electricity: Explores how satellites built in Glasgow are powered by solar panels.

regions.default: Swaps in examples from Glasgow’s space and engineering industries.
regions.demoLine: Satellites built in Glasgow run on solar panels, turning light into electrical energy. The city builds more small satellites than anywhere else in Europe.

regions.name: Belfast
facts: The Giant’s Causeway on the Antrim coast is made of around 40,000 basalt columns.
Belfast’s shipyard built the Titanic. Its yellow cranes, Samson and Goliath, still dominate the skyline.
Northern Ireland has a growing aerospace and cyber security industry.

topics.Rocks and fossils: Uses the Giant’s Causeway’s basalt columns to explore igneous rock.
topics.Materials: Links materials to the ships and aircraft parts made in Belfast.
topics.Wind energy: Uses wind farms on the Antrim hills and coast as the worked example.
topics.Electricity: Follows electricity from Northern Ireland’s wind farms to Belfast homes.

regions.default: Swaps in examples from Belfast’s engineering, aerospace and coastline.
regions.demoLine: Wind farms on the Antrim hills and coast now supply a large share of Northern Ireland’s electricity.

regions.name: South Wales
facts: South Wales has one of the world’s first compound semiconductor clusters, making chips for phones and electric cars.
The South Wales coalfield shaped the country’s industry for over a century.
The Cardiff Bay barrage turned a tidal bay into a freshwater lake.

topics.Electricity: Links circuits to the computer chips made in South Wales.
topics.Circuits: Links circuits to the computer chips made in South Wales.
topics.Rocks and fossils: Uses the South Wales coalfield to explore how rocks and fuels form.
topics.Energy transfers: Compares coal, the region’s past, with tidal and wind energy, its future.

regions.default: Swaps in examples from South Wales’ semiconductor, energy and coastal industries.
regions.demoLine: South Wales once powered the world with coal. Now it’s investing in wind and tidal energy along its coast.

regions.name: Manchester
facts: Graphene, the world’s thinnest material, was first isolated at the University of Manchester in 2004.
Manchester grew into one of the world’s first industrial cities, powered by cotton mills.
The world’s first stored-program computer ran in Manchester in 1948.

topics.Materials: Uses graphene, first isolated in Manchester, as the super-material example.
topics.Electricity: Links electricity to Manchester’s computing history, from 1948 to today.
topics.Scientists: Adds Manchester scientists, from John Dalton to the graphene team.

regions.default: Swaps in examples from Manchester’s science, computing and industrial history.
regions.demoLine: Manchester’s mills once ran on steam. Today, researchers there are exploring how graphene could make lighter, stronger materials and better batteries.

regions.name: the West Midlands
regions.place: Birmingham, Coventry and the West Midlands
facts: Coventry is home to the UK Battery Industrialisation Centre, which helps develop batteries for electric vehicles.
The West Midlands is a centre for car making, from classic engineering to electric vehicles.
James Watt and Matthew Boulton built steam engines in Birmingham in the 1700s.

topics.Electricity: Uses electric vehicle batteries developed in the West Midlands as the example.
topics.Circuits: Uses electric vehicle batteries developed in the West Midlands as the example.
topics.Energy transfers: Compares Birmingham’s steam engines with today’s electric cars.
topics.Robotics: Links robots to car factories across the West Midlands.

regions.default: Swaps in examples from the West Midlands’ car-making and engineering industries.
regions.demoLine: Engineers in Coventry help develop the batteries that store wind-generated electricity for electric cars.

regions.name: Cornwall
facts: United Downs, near Redruth, is the UK’s first deep geothermal power plant.
Cornwall is exploring lithium extraction for electric car batteries.
Cornwall’s mining landscape is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

topics.Rocks and fossils: Uses Cornish granite and the county’s tin and copper mining heritage.
topics.Electricity: Links electricity to geothermal power at United Downs, near Redruth.
topics.Energy transfers: Uses geothermal heat from deep below Cornwall as the energy source.
topics.Living things and habitats: Uses Cornish rockpools as the habitat study.

regions.default: Swaps in examples from Cornwall’s coast, geology and new energy industries.
regions.demoLine: Cornwall’s windy coast and deep hot granite make it a test-bed for new energy, from wind turbines to geothermal power at United Downs.

regions.name: London
facts: Engineers spent over a decade building the Elizabeth line tunnels under London.
London is a world centre for medical research, including the Francis Crick Institute.
The Thames Barrier protects the city from tidal flooding.

topics.Materials: Uses the Elizabeth line’s tunnels as the materials and engineering example.
topics.Human body: Links to medical research at London’s science institutes.
topics.Food and nutrition: Links to nutrition research at London’s science institutes.
topics.Waves: Uses the Thames Barrier to explore tides and waves.

regions.default: Swaps in examples from London’s engineering, transport and medical research.
regions.demoLine: The London Array, in the Thames Estuary, helps power homes across the capital.
